aiAgentFacts.fact: In a retrospective case-control study of 50,787 middle-aged neutered client-owned dogs across 12 breeds, dogs in overweight body condition had a shorter median life span than dogs in normal body condition in every breed examined.
Hazard ratios for death in overweight versus normal-condition dogs ranged from 1.35 (German Shepherd Dog, 99.79% CI 1.05–1.73) to 2.86 (Yorkshire Terrier, 99.79% CI 2.14–3.83).
Yorkshire Terriers showed the largest median life-span gap: 13.7 years in overweight condition versus 16.2 years in normal condition.
German Shepherd Dogs showed the smallest median life-span gap: 12.1 years in overweight condition versus 12.5 years in normal condition.
The elevated risk of death in overweight dogs was present throughout the age range studied, not only at advanced ages.
The study's authors concluded that veterinary professionals should promote healthy body condition particularly from midlife onward.
This study tested no weight-loss intervention; it cannot support any claim that reducing a dog's weight extends life span.
The study population was restricted to neutered client-owned dogs of 12 breeds in North America; mixed-breed and unneutered dogs were not represented.

historyQuestions: Not specified by this paper. The study uses recorded body condition as an exposure variable and prescribes no owner-facing history questions.
redFlags: Not addressed — this study does not identify red-flag symptoms warranting urgent referral.
differentialDiagnosesMentioned: Not addressed — the study measures the association between recorded body condition and life span, not differential diagnosis.
recommendedDiagnosticWorkups: The study's own exposure measure: veterinarian-assigned body condition recorded at routine visits, as distinct from scale weight alone.

limitations: Design-level: retrospective case-control from clinical records — establishes association, never causation
Design-level: no weight-loss intervention was tested, so no conclusion about the effect of weight reduction is supported
Uncontrolled confounding: occult illness can independently drive both body condition change and mortality; the design cannot separate this from a weight effect
Exposure classification relied on body condition as recorded in routine clinical practice rather than a standardized research re-assessment
Generalizability: neutered client-owned dogs, 12 breeds, North America only — excludes mixed-breed and unneutered populations
Effect size varied more than sixfold across breeds (HR 1.35 to 2.86), so a single population-level figure would misrepresent any individual breed
